parts.title: My first debate
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last term, my teacher asked me to join the school debating team. I said no at first, because I hate speaking in front of people. But she told me that I was good at arguing with my brother, so I decided to try.

Our first debate was against another school, and the subject was "Zoos should be closed". We were given the side against zoos. I did not agree with it, but our coach said that a good debater can argue for any idea. This surprised me.

I spoke second. My notes were shaking in my hands, and my voice was a whisper. But after a minute, I forgot my nerves and started to enjoy myself. I gave three reasons and an example, and I looked at the judges, as I had been taught.

We lost the debate, but one of the judges said that my speech was the clearest. That made me happy. I have learned that listening is just as important as speaking, and I now understand other people's opinions much better.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer decide to join the team?
options: Her friends were all in it
She had won a speech prize
She wanted to win a prize
questions.explanation: Her teacher said she was good at arguing with her brother.

questions.explanation: She did not agree with her side, but a good debater can argue for any idea.

questions.prompt: How did she feel when she began to speak?
questions.explanation: Her notes were shaking and her voice was a whisper.

questions.prompt: What happened after a minute?
questions.explanation: She forgot her nerves and started to enjoy herself.

questions.prompt: What has she learned?
options: Judges are always right about everything
Winning is the most important thing of all
Listening is as important as speaking
questions.explanation: Listening is just as important as speaking.

parts.title: How to give a good speech
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Many people are afraid of speaking in public, but it is a skill that anyone can learn. [1] Here are some simple tips to help you.

First, know your audience. Think about who will be listening and what they want to hear. [2] A talk to young children, for example, should be very different from a talk to teachers.

Second, keep it short and clear. Most listeners remember only two or three main ideas. [3] Everything else just makes your message harder to follow.

Third, speak slowly. When we are nervous, we speak very fast. [4] Take a breath at the end of each sentence, and you will sound much more confident.

Finally, practise out loud. Stand in front of a mirror, or ask a friend to listen. [5] The more you rehearse, the less afraid you will be on the day.
sentences: This makes it difficult for the audience to understand you.
Your hands should always stay in your pockets.
The same words will not work for every group of people.
It may feel strange at first, but it really works.
Speakers who read from paper often forget to look up.
Choose these carefully and repeat them at the end.
Do not forget to wear comfortable shoes.
All it takes is a little preparation and a lot of practice.

gaps.explanation: All it takes is a little preparation, and the next sentence gives tips.
The same words will not work for every group, and the example follows.
Choose the main ideas carefully; everything else makes the message harder.
Fast speech makes it hard to understand, and the next sentence advises taking a breath.
It may feel strange, and the next sentence says the more you rehearse the less afraid you are.

parts.title: A note about the debate
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Dear Lena, I just wanted to say congratulations on your speech yesterday! You were so calm and clear that nobody could [1] that you were nervous. I especially liked the part [2] you told the story about your first day at school. Everyone laughed, and I think that this helped the judges to [3] you. Our team did not win, [4] I am sure that we will do better next time. Mrs Blake said that we should practise our answers to difficult questions. I [5] already started to write mine. Are you free on Thursday after lessons? We could meet in the library and work together [6] our next debate. See you soon, Jory

parts.title: A great speaker
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Martin Luther King was one of the greatest speakers in history. He gave his most famous speech in 1963, [1] he spoke to more than two hundred thousand people in Washington. He talked about his dream that one day, all people would be treated [2] same. He did not read from paper for most of the speech. Instead, he spoke from his heart, [3] his voice rose and fell like music. He also used short, simple sentences and repeated the words "I have a dream" again and again. This made it easy for people to remember. Speech experts say that his talk is a perfect example [4] how to speak in public. Thousands of students study it every year, and many people can still say parts of it by heart. His words continue to inspire people all [5] the world, long after his death. It shows that a good speech can change the way people think, and this is [6] we remember it today.

gaps.explanation: In 1963, when he spoke to 200,000 people: relative of time.
"Treated the same" is a fixed phrase: everybody gets equal treatment.
He spoke from his heart, and his voice rose and fell.
An example of how to speak: a fixed phrase.
All over the world: a fixed phrase.
This is why we remember it: the reason.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good evening, everybody. When Mr Dean asked us to give a speech about a person that we admire, I thought about a lot of names. First I thought of a famous writer, because I have read all her books twice. Then I thought of our head teacher, who is here tonight, and I hope she isn’t offended. But in the end, I chose the woman who taught me to read when I was four. She had no university degree and she never travelled far from her village. She made soup every Sunday, and she told me stories that she made up as she went. This speech is for my grandmother.

options: The head teacher of the school
question.explanation: He considered a writer and the head teacher, but he chose the woman who taught him to read and told him stories, his grandmother.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Keir, is the debate in the main hall? I saw a poster there.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That was the old poster. The hall is full of chairs for the exams, so they moved it. I thought of the library, but they have a book fair this week.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So where is it?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Room twelve, the biggest classroom on the second floor. The judges are already there, I saw them.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Thanks. I’ll tell Mia. She’s looking for the entrance of the hall.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good, because she’s going to be late.

question.explanation: The poster in the hall is old because of the exams and the library has a book fair, so the debate is in room twelve.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: You look so happy, Leah! Did you win?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: No, I came third, and the winner was from the north. That’s fine. And I didn’t talk to the famous speaker who was on the list, because he left early.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So why the smile?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I never needed my notes, not once. Last time I held my cards like a shield and read most of it. Today I knew every word.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s great.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I know. My teacher cried a little, and she is usually so serious. Will you come to the next round and clap for me?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Of course, I wouldn’t miss it.

question.explanation: She came third and did not meet the famous speaker, but she did not need her notes at all, which she did last time.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Mum says you spend hours in the bathroom. Are you hiding from your brothers?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’m practising my speech. It’s the only room with a lock, but that’s not the reason.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Is it because it’s quiet? The house is so noisy.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Not quiet at all, the tap is dripping. But with all those tiles my voice sounds deep and clear, like in a theatre. And I know there’s a big mirror, but I can’t look at it, because it makes me laugh.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Then maybe you should practise in the garden.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Not a chance. The neighbours would hear.

question.prompt: Why does the boy practise in the bathroom?
question.explanation: He says the room is not quiet and he cannot look at the mirror; the tiles make his voice sound deep and clear.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Right, class, a few words about your speeches for Friday. Last year they were about ten minutes, but that was for the older students, so forget it. I know some of you want five or six minutes, because a good topic needs time. I understand that, but the judges have only four minutes for each person. So please make it three or four, no more. If you finish early, nobody minds, but if you go over, I will stop you. Practise with a clock at home, and bring your cards on Thursday so that I can check them.

question.prompt: How long should the speech be?
question.explanation: Ten minutes was for the older students and five or six is too long for the judges; the limit is four minutes, so three or four.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Your speech was fantastic, Keir. Did your coach help you? He’s famous for training champions.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I did go to him once, but he only said, "Be yourself," and that was it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Your brother then? He’s studying law.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: He wanted to help, but he’s always travelling, and we only talked on the phone for five minutes. The real help was my aunt. She used to teach drama, and she showed me where to breathe, where to look and where to stop.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: She must be proud.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: She cried more than my mum did.

question.prompt: Who gave the man tips for his speech?
question.explanation: The coach only said "Be yourself" and the brother is always away; the person who taught him to breathe, look and stop was his aunt.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Great speech! Are you going home to rest now?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I thought I would, because I’m exhausted. But the team insisted. We’re going for pizza, because the coach is paying.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Brilliant. Then you start work on the new speech?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: On Monday, not today. Today I just want to celebrate. I haven’t eaten anything since breakfast, and I was too nervous.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Save me a slice, then.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Come with us! There’s a big table, and the others would love to see you. We’ll sit near the window and talk about the next round.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: All right, if you’re sure.

question.prompt: What will the girl do afterwards?
question.explanation: She wanted to go home but the team insisted on pizza; she will start the new speech on Monday.

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: f

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: f

question.explanation: He thinks the topic was easy and she does not; the judges were strange but not unfair, and both think the girls from Westfield deserved to win.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Be honest, Kaya. How was my speech?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You did very well, honestly. Your voice was strong, and I could hear every word in the last row.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: And the ending? I rushed it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Yes, you spoke very quickly at the end and I missed a joke. But everybody laughed at the others, and you didn’t forget anything.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I felt my knees shake.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Nobody could see. Just slow down next time, take a breath between the ideas, and smile a little more.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’ll try. Thanks for telling me the truth.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s what friends are for.

question.prompt: What does the woman say about his speech?
options: It was good but too fast
question.explanation: She heard every word and he forgot nothing, but the ending was fast and she missed a joke.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Congratulations, captain! I heard Mr Dean chose you.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Thanks. I can’t believe it. Jo was the obvious choice, and I thought she would get it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Aren’t you worried? There’s a lot of work, and training twice a week.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: A bit, but I like organising things. I’m so excited. I’ve been smiling since this morning and I can’t stop. Honestly, I’d do it for free.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Well, you will! Who’s going to be your vice-captain?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I don’t know yet. I’ll ask the team on Monday.

question.prompt: How does the man feel about being captain?
question.explanation: He is surprised that he was chosen over Jo and is a little worried about the work, but mostly he cannot stop smiling and would do it for free.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Leah, I’m thinking of joining the speaking club. Is it any good?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It’s great. Is it to improve your marks? Mr Ash gives extra points for joining.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That would be nice, but no. And I have plenty of friends. The real thing is that my hands shake every time I speak in front of the class. I get so nervous, and I want that to stop.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It will get better. I was the same in my first year, and now I don’t even think about it.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Really? Then I’ll go on Tuesday and ask Mr Ash about the next meeting.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Good. I’ll walk there with you.

question.prompt: Why does the man want to join the speaking club?
question.explanation: He says marks and friends are not the reason; he wants his hands to stop shaking because he is nervous in front of the class.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The debate has started, Levi. The door is closed.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Should we wait here until they finish the first speech?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That might take twenty minutes. Let’s go in quietly and sit at the back. Nobody will mind.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: And speak to the judges first? To say sorry?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Afterwards. Come on.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: OK, but I’ll open the door slowly. The last time I went in late, the door made a terrible noise and everybody looked at me.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That was in the library! Just come.

question.prompt: What do the friends decide to do?
options: Go in and sit at the back
question.explanation: Waiting would take twenty minutes and they will speak to the judges afterwards, so they go in quietly and sit at the back.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Jory, you’re pale. Is the speech too long again?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, I timed it, four minutes exactly. And I have my cards here, all eight, in the right order.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So what’s the matter?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I tried the microphone ten minutes ago, and it kept making a noise, then it stopped. If it doesn’t work, nobody will hear me in the last row.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The technician is coming. Don’t worry.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I hope he’s quick, because the first speech is in ten minutes and I’m the second.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You will be fine. Drink some water.

question.prompt: What is the boy worried about?
question.explanation: The speech takes four minutes and the cards are in order; he fears that the microphone will stop and nobody will hear him.

parts.title: A talk about a debating competition
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: nathalie
turns.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I’m Lena, the captain of the school debating team, and today I’d like to tell you about our competition next month. It will be on the fourteenth of November. The practice round is a week earlier, on the seventh, but only the teams come to that. The competition will be in our school hall. Last year twelve schools took part, which was too many, and we finished at nine in the evening. So this year we invited only eight schools. Each team has three speakers. Every speaker talks for four minutes, and after that there are two minutes for questions. People often forget the second number, but it matters. The topic is different from other years. In the past the teams knew it a week before, but now we give it to them one hour before the debate, so there is no time to learn a speech by heart. They must think quickly. A team of judges, with two teachers and a former student, will decide the winner. The winning team receives a silver cup, and the runners-up get bronze medals. Now, for those who would like to watch. Entry is free, and you don’t have to book. The debate starts at ten, but the doors open at half past eight. Please come before half past nine, because we close the doors after that, so nobody disturbs the speakers. Our own team will wear the green school jumper, so you can see us easily and clap when we come in. Finally, there will be sandwiches and tea at lunchtime for everyone in the canteen, and the students from the other schools can try our famous lemon cake. Thank you very much.

gaps.prompt: The competition takes place on November the ___
gaps.explanation: The practice round is on the seventh, but the competition is on the fourteenth.

gaps.prompt: This year ___ schools will take part
gaps.explanation: Twelve schools came last year, but this year they invited only eight.

gaps.prompt: Each speaker can talk for ___ minutes
gaps.explanation: After the four minutes of the speech there are two minutes for questions.

gaps.prompt: The team gets the topic ___ hour before the debate
gaps.explanation: In the past the topic was known a week before, but now it is given one hour before.

gaps.prompt: The winning team takes home a silver ___
gaps.explanation: The winners get a silver cup and the runners-up get bronze medals.

gaps.prompt: Spectators have to come before half past ___
gaps.explanation: The debate starts at ten and the doors open at half past eight, but visitors must arrive before half past nine.

parts.title: An interview with a debating coach
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Keir, why do you enjoy coaching?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: People think I’ll say winning, and of course trophies are nice, we have a few cups. And I have been to several countries with teams, which I love, but I would never choose a job for the travel. What gets me is watching a student who couldn’t ask a question in class last September stand up in front of two hundred people and speak. At that moment I’m proud and a bit emotional.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the first thing you teach?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Many beginners think it’s about talking, and some buy a suit before the first lesson, but the way you dress is the last thing. I don’t start with writing either, because you can type fast and still say nothing. We begin with listening. If you don’t hear what the other team really says, you can’t answer. I make them repeat each other’s arguments before they reply.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why do you give students a side?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Because it’s the best lesson. Some days a student has to defend an idea that they hate. It doesn’t make the debates shorter, they are exactly the same length, and we have the occasional argument in the corridor, so that isn’t the reason. But when you defend the other side, you see why somebody believes it, and you stop thinking that they are stupid.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What mistake do you see most often?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Speaking too fast and trying to say everything. Nervous students put ten ideas into four minutes, and the judges remember none. I tell them: three ideas, well explained. Arguing with the judges has happened only once, and missing practice is a problem for a few, but it’s rare.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you do the day before a competition?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I used to give them a day off to relax, but they just worried more. A trip to the theatre was a nice idea for a while, and I took them once, but it did nothing. Now we have a mock debate with parents and teachers as the audience. It feels real, and it takes their fear away.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Apart from confidence, what do students gain?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Some people think it would help with dates and facts, and I would love to say that, but their memory isn’t better than anybody else’s. A few go on to act, but only because they were already good at it. The biggest change, and the one that parents notice, is respect. They learn to listen to opinions that they don’t share, even at home, around the dinner table.

questions.prompt: What does Keir like most about his work?
options: Watching shy students find their voice
questions.explanation: Trophies and travel are nice, but he is proud and emotional when a student who could not ask a question speaks to two hundred people.

questions.prompt: What does Keir teach first?
questions.explanation: Clothes are the last thing and fast writing is not the start; they begin with listening to the other team.

questions.prompt: Why does Keir give students a side?
questions.explanation: The debates are the same length and arguments in the corridor still happen; defending the other side shows why people believe it.

questions.prompt: What mistake does he see most often?
options: Speaking too fast and saying too much
questions.explanation: Arguing with the judges happened once and missing practice is rare; nervous students put ten ideas into four minutes.

questions.prompt: What does he do the day before a competition?
options: Gives the students a day off
questions.explanation: The day off made them worry and the theatre did nothing; now they have a mock debate with parents and teachers.

questions.prompt: What do students gain apart from confidence?
questions.explanation: Their memory is not better and only a few act, but they learn to listen to opinions that they do not share.

parts.title: Getting to know you
parts.instructions: Answer each question in your own words. Aim to speak for 20-30 seconds.

questions.prompt: Do you like speaking in front of other people? Why or why not?
